# Lecture #44: Introduction to Ophthalmology

**Lecturer:** A. Nattis, D.O.
**Session:** Lecture #44

## Pupil Abnormalities

### Horner's Syndrome

:::correlate
**Horner's Syndrome Triad**
*   **Ptosis** (droopy upper lid)
*   **Miosis** (small pupil)
*   **Anhidrosis** (lack of sweating on forehead above affected eye)

**Etiology:**
*   **Preganglionic:** Hypothalamus → Superior cervical ganglion. Vertebrobasilar stroke, vertebral artery dissection, cervical disc disease.
*   **Postganglionic:** Superior cervical ganglion → Iris dilator. **Internal carotid artery dissection** (most common/severe), cavernous sinus disease, herpes zoster, parotid/nasopharynx tumors.

**Workup:** Any suspected Horner's → Neural workup (rule out dissection, stroke, tumor).
:::

### Hutchinson's Pupil
*   **Presentation:** Unilateral dilated, poorly reactive pupil in **comatose patient**.
*   **Cause:** Ipsilateral supratentorial mass → Uncal herniation → CN III compression.

## Ocular Muscle Disorders

### Myasthenia Gravis

:::correlate
**Myasthenia Gravis**
*   **Mechanism:** Autoantibodies block Ach receptors at motor endplates.
*   **Hallmark:** **Fatigability** (symptoms worsen throughout day).
*   **Ocular:** 90% have eye symptoms. Ptosis, diplopia, limited EOM, eye fatigue.
    *   50% with ocular symptoms → 80% develop generalized disease.
*   **Diagnosis:** **Tensilon test** (Edrophonium IV, AchE inhibitor → Stronger muscle contraction. 80-90% positive). Rest test.
*   **Note:** May cause severe bradycardia → Give 1-2mg test dose first, have atropine available.
:::

### Thyroid-Related Ophthalmopathy

:::correlate
**Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)**
*   **Pathology:** GAG infiltration into EOMs → Proptosis.
*   **Presentation:** Dry eye, redness, pain, restriction of motility, optic nerve compression.
*   **Note:** Even with controlled hormone levels, stigma of TED persists.
:::

### Myotonic Dystrophy
*   **Genetics:** Autosomal dominant (Chr 19).
*   **Features:** Myotonia of peripheral muscles (worsens with cold, excitement, fatigue). **Christmas tree cataract**, pigmentary retinopathy, ptosis, lid lag.

### Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)
*   **Cause:** Mitochondrial disease.
*   **Kearns-Sayre Syndrome:** Ophthalmoplegia + ptosis + retinal pigment degeneration + heart block.

## Optic Neuropathies

### Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis)

:::highyield
**Giant Cell Arteritis**
*   **Population:** Age >55, F>M (2:1).
*   **Pathology:** Inflammatory vasculopathy of medium-large vessels. Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells.
*   **Presentation:**
    *   **Arteritic ION:** Acute painless vision loss, ± amaurosis fugax/diplopia.
    *   **Systemic:** Scalp tenderness, **jaw claudication**, joint pain (polymyalgia rheumatica), fever, malaise, anorexia, weight loss, headache, tender temporal artery ± ↓ pulsation, neck pain, brainstem CVA.
*   **Diagnosis:** ↑ ESR, ↑ CRP, ↓ HCT, thrombocytosis. **Temporal artery biopsy** (confirmatory).
*   **Treatment:** **Steroids ASAP** (Prednisone 60-100mg PO ± IV) to prevent fellow eye involvement (65% risk within 10 days without treatment).
:::

### Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION)

:::correlate
**AION**
*   **Mechanism:** Infarct of optic nerve head (posterior ciliary arteries) → Acute painless vision loss.
*   **Findings:** ↓ Color vision, ↓ VA, RAPD, VF loss, unilateral optic disc edema.
*   **Types:**
    *   **Arteritic ION:** Giant cell arteritis (see above).
    *   **Nonarteritic ION (NAION):** 50-75 y/o, **normal ESR**. Associated with DM, microvascular disease. Recurrence in same eye rare. 25-40% fellow eye involvement.
:::

### Posterior ION
*   **Mechanism:** ↓ Blood flow/oxygenation to intraorbital optic nerve.
*   **Causes:** Hypotension (volume loss), ↑ peripheral vascular resistance, ↑ venous pressure (orbital edema), ↑ IOP, ↓ O₂ carrying capacity.

### Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)

:::correlate
**Pseudotumor Cerebri**
*   **Population:** 90% female, mean age 33, associated with **obesity**.
*   **Presentation:** Papilledema with **normal neuroimaging and CSF**. HA, N/V, optic disc edema, transient visual obscurations, photopsias, VF defect, retrobulbar pain, pulsatile tinnitus, ± diplopia, RAPD.
*   **Diagnosis:** ↑ CSF pressure with normal composition (diagnosis of exclusion).
*   **Etiology:** Endocrinopathy, COPD, dural sinus thrombosis, steroids, OCPs, Vitamin A, tetracycline, nalidixic acid, isotretinoin.
*   **Treatment:**
    *   **No vision loss:** HA treatment, weight loss.
    *   **Mild vision loss:** Acetazolamide (Diamox), furosemide, weight loss.
    *   **Advanced vision/VF loss:** Optic nerve sheath decompression, serial LPs, lumbar-peritoneal shunt.
:::

### Optic Neuritis

:::highyield
**Optic Neuritis**
*   **Population:** Most common optic neuropathy in patients <45 y/o.
*   **Presentation:** Acute unilateral vision loss (may recover spontaneously), **ocular pain on eye movement**, ↓ color vision, RAPD, VF defect, optic nerve appears swollen or normal.
*   **Uhthoff's phenomenon:** Worsening symptoms with heat/exercise.
*   **Phosphenes:** Flashes of light induced by eye movements or sound.
*   **DDx:** Idiopathic, **MS** (most common), syphilis, sarcoidosis, Lyme, Wegener's, SLE, Devic's.
*   **MS Link:** **30% develop MS within 4 years; 38% within 10 years**. Always monitor neurologically.
:::

## Red Eyelids

### Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO)

:::correlate
**Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus**
*   **Presentation:** Unilateral painful skin rash in dermatomal distribution (trigeminal nerve). Vesicles crust/heal in 2-6 weeks.
*   **Hutchinson's sign:** Skin lesions at tip, side, or root of nose → Strong predictor of **ocular involvement** (nasociliary nerve).
*   **Population:** >60 y/o (can occur any age). Latent VZV reactivation in sensory ganglia. HIV patients 15x more likely.
*   **Prodrome:** Fever, malaise, HA, eye pain prior to rash.
*   **Management:**
    *   **Oral antivirals** (acyclovir, famciclovir, valacyclovir) for ≥10 days. Immunosuppressed may need IV.
    *   **Topical antibiotic ointment** (prevent superinfection).
    *   **Topical steroids** (keratitis/uveitis). **PO/IV steroids** (scleritis, retinitis, choroiditis, optic neuritis).
    *   **Amitriptyline 25mg PO** for neuropathic pain.
*   **Prevention:** Shingles vaccine recommended for patients >60 y/o.
:::

## Red Eyeball

### Conjunctivitis

**Viral (Most common infectious):**
*   **Adenovirus:** Highly contagious, 5-12 day incubation. Watery discharge, ± lid swelling.
*   **HSV-1:** Skin lesions may be present.

**Allergic:**
*   **Presentation:** Lid swelling, diffuse redness, chemosis. Most frequent in spring/summer.
*   **Treatment:** Allergen avoidance, cold compresses, artificial tears, topical steroid, antihistamine (gtts/PO).

**Bacterial (2nd most common):**
*   **Presentation:** Red eye, purulent/mucopurulent discharge, chemosis, ↓ VA, ± lid swelling. Usually 7-10 days.
*   **Organisms:** *N. gonorrhoeae* (**risk of corneal perforation** → IM Ceftriaxone 1g + lavage), *N. meningitidis*, *S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*.
*   **COVID-19:** Can present as conjunctivitis.
*   **Treatment:** Hand hygiene, symptomatic (cold compresses, artificial tears), broad-spectrum antibiotic gtts.

### Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma

:::highyield
**Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma**
*   **Presentation:** Acute eye pain, blurry vision (in dark room/dim lighting), mid-dilated pupil, corneal edema, ↑ IOP.
*   **Mechanism:** Iris blocks trabecular meshwork → ↑ IOP → Risk of vision loss (chokes off blood supply to optic nerve).
*   **Emergency Treatment:**
    *   **Eye drops** to ↓ IOP.
    *   **IV Acetazolamide** + **mannitol**.
    *   **Definitive:** **Laser peripheral iridotomy** (make small opening in iris to allow aqueous drainage).
:::

### Uveitis

:::correlate
**Uveitis**
*   **Presentation:** Dull, achy pain, photophobia, blurry vision, ± floaters.
*   **Etiology:** Autoimmune (most common), infectious (Hepatitis C, syphilis less common).
*   **Workup:** History of autoimmune conditions? Exposure to infectious diseases? Comprehensive ophthalmic exam. Partner with rheumatology/infectious disease.
*   **Treatment:** **Steroids** (topical gtts usually sufficient; may need subtenon/intraocular injections or oral steroids).
:::

## Decreased Vision

### Cataracts
*   **Definition:** Opacification of crystalline lens. **Most common cause:** Age-related.
*   **Other Causes:** Corticosteroids, drugs, trauma, diabetes, myotonic dystrophy, **Wilson's disease** (sunflower cataract), ocular disease (uveitis, myopia).
*   **Treatment:** Cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation.

### Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)

**Dry AMD (90%):**
*   **Pathology:** Drusen (yellow deposits) at back of eye.
*   **Management:** Mild disease → Follow, recommend antioxidant vitamins. Many do fine long-term.

**Wet AMD (10%, more severe):**
*   **Pathology:** Abnormal blood vessels grow under retina → Weak, prone to bleeding.
*   **Treatment:** Injections of medication into back of eye to regress vessels.

### Diabetic Retinopathy

:::highyield
**Diabetic Retinopathy**
*   **Epidemiology:** 80% of patients with diabetes develop this after 20 years. Leading cause of blindness in patients aged 20-64.
*   **Presentation:** Microaneurysms (small findings) → Retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, neovascularization (severe).
*   **Treatment:** **Glycemic control** (underlying). Laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF injections depending on severity.
:::

### Retinal Detachment

:::correlate
**Retinal Detachment**
*   **Classic Symptoms:** **Flashes and floaters**. Curtain/shadow across vision.
*   **Mechanism:** Retina peels off from back of eye.
*   **Risk Factors:** Nearsightedness, eye surgery, trauma, family history, severe diabetic eye disease.
*   **Management:** Small tears → Laser in office. Larger detachments → **Vitrectomy surgery** (retina surgeon tacks retina back down).
*   **Important:** Neurosurgical/ophthalmologic emergency.
:::

## Double Vision

**Causes:**
*   **CN III, IV, VI palsies** (trauma, stroke, compression, microvascular disease).
*   **Myasthenia gravis** (fatigability).
*   **Thyroid eye disease** (EOM restriction).
*   **Retroorbital mass** (tumor behind eye).
*   **Strabismus surgery** may be needed to strengthen EOMs.

## Systemic Diseases with Ocular Findings

*   **Autoimmune diseases:** Associated with uveitis.
*   **Peripheral ulcerative keratitis:** Thinning of cornea (rheumatoid arthritis → May need corneal-scleral graft).
*   **Wilson's disease:** Sunflower cataract, Kayser-Fleischer rings.
*   **HIV retinopathy:** Looks like diabetic retinopathy (cotton-wool spots).

## Ophthalmology
### Pupil Abnormalities
*   **Horner's**: Ptosis, Miosis, Anhidrosis (ICA dissection)
*   **Hutchinson's**: Dilated (uncal herniation)
### Ocular Muscle Disorders
*   **Myasthenia gravis**: Fatigability, Tensilon test
*   **Thyroid eye disease**: Proptosis, GAG infiltration
### Optic Neuropathies
*   **Temporal arteritis**: Jaw claudication, steroids ASAP
*   **Optic neuritis**: Pain on movement, 30% → MS
*   **Pseudotumor**: Obese female, normal MRI
### Red Eye
*   **HZO**: Hutchinson's sign, antivirals
*   **Acute glaucoma**: Laser iridotomy
*   **Uveitis**: Autoimmune, steroids
### Decreased Vision
*   **Diabetic retinopathy**: Leading blindness 20-64
*   **Retinal detachment**: Flashes/floaters
*   **AMD**: Drusen (dry), neovascularization (wet)
